title: Multimedia Project
text:
Where to Start
Read the Welcome page, then move on to the Build and deploy overview. The overview shows the whole process in one diagram and lists the seven steps you will follow.

title: 4. Feature branches and pull requests
text:
Who: every team member, one at a time. Goal: each of you adds your name to the site’s footer through your own branch and pull request, reviewed and merged by a teammate.
The footer is a good first change: it is one small file, it appears on every page, and you will see your name on the test server a few minutes after your pull request is merged. Everyone edits the same few lines of that file, so take turns: the next person starts only after the previous pull request is merged. Later, when you work on different files, you can work in parallel.

title: 4. Feature branches and pull requests
text:
The cycle





flowchart LR
  A["Pull develop"] --> B["Branch"] --> C["Change + run locally"] --> D["Commit + push"] --> E["Pull request"] --> F["CI green +<br/>teammate review"] --> G["Merge"] --> H["Auto-deploy<br/>to test"]

title: 4. Feature branches and pull requests
text:
4.1 Create an issue
On your team’s project board, create an issue such as Add Aoife to the footer and assign it to yourself. Note its number, e.g. #7.

title: 4. Feature branches and pull requests
text:
4.2 Start from the latest develop
git switch develop
git pull
git switch -c feature/7-add-aoife-to-footer
Branch names follow feature/<issue-number>-<short-description>. In IntelliJ: Git → Pull, then click the branch name bottom right → New Branch.

title: 4. Feature branches and pull requests
4. Feature branches and pull requests
text:
4.4 Commit and push
git status
git add src/main/resources/templates/fragments/footer.html
git commit -m "Add Aoife to the footer (#7)"
git push -u origin feature/7-add-aoife-to-footer
git status should list only footer.html. Never commit .idea/, target/ or anything with a password in it.

title: 4. Feature branches and pull requests
text:
4.5 Open the pull request
On GitHub, click Compare & pull request on the yellow banner, or Pull requests → New pull request.

base: develop ← compare: your branch. Never main.
Title: what the change does, e.g. Add Aoife to the footer. This title appears in the test server’s footer once it is merged, so make it readable.
Description: Closes #7, how to check it (the footer on any page), and a screenshot.
Reviewers: one teammate.

The ci check starts straight away. Wait for the green tick. A red cross does not stop the Merge button from working, so do not rely on GitHub to catch it. If it goes red, click Details, read the log, fix it on the same branch and push again: the pull request updates itself.

title: 4. Feature branches and pull requests
text:
4.6 Review a teammate’s pull request
Reviewing means running the change, not just reading it. With db running:
git fetch origin
git switch feature/7-add-aoife-to-footer
./mvnw spring-boot:run
Check the footer on the home page and the login page, then on GitHub open Files changed:

Does it do what the issue says, and nothing else?
Is the HTML valid, with every <li> closed and the list still inside the <footer>?
Are any unexpected files changed or deleted?

If it is fine, choose Review changes → Approve. Otherwise choose Request changes with a comment saying exactly what to fix. Afterwards, stop the app and switch back with git switch develop.

title: 4. Feature branches and pull requests
text:
4.7 Merge
When ci is green and the review is approved, the author clicks Squash and merge, then Delete branch. Squashing keeps develop’s history to one commit per feature.






ImportantTeam rules



GitHub does not enforce these in your team repo: the Merge button works whatever the checks say, and anyone can push straight to develop or main. Your team keeps them:

Merge only when ci shows a green tick.
Merge only after a teammate has approved the pull request. Never approve or merge your own work without a review.
Never push straight to develop or main. Every change goes through a pull request.

Each pull request records its checks, its review and who merged it, so your lecturer can see whether the rules were kept.


The merge into develop starts deploy-test on the test server. Step 5 checks it: the footer there will show your pull request’s title and your name.

title: 4. Feature branches and pull requests
section: 4.8 Hand over to the next person
text:
4.8 Hand over to the next person
Tell the next teammate the pull request is merged. They start again at 4.2; git pull brings your change into their develop, so they will find the list and add their line below yours.






NoteIf you get a merge conflict





If two people edited the same lines, GitHub reports This branch has conflicts. On your branch:
git switch develop
git pull
git switch feature/7-add-aoife-to-footer
git merge develop
Open footer.html. Keep both names in the list, keep only one <ul class="team-list"> and one </ul>, and delete the <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> lines. Run the app to check the footer, then commit and push. The pull request updates and CI runs again.









TipCheckpoint



Every member has one merged pull request, approved by a teammate, and the footer on develop lists every member of the team.

title: 7. Check the prod deployment
text: Who: the whole team. Goal: confirm the release is running on prod, and know how to roll back if it is not.

title: 7. Check the prod deployment
text:
7.1 Follow the deployment
Open Actions → deploy-prod. The newest run is named after your tag, e.g. v0.1.0. Check that:

Check the tag is on main passed
Start the database ends with Database is up
Wait for the app to answer ends with Release v0.1.0 is up
The run’s summary shows Release v0.1.0 deployed, with a link to the prod site

If the run stays Queued with Waiting for a runner, the prod server is stopped: tell your lecturer.

title: 7. Check the prod deployment
text:
7.2 Check it in the browser
The run’s summary shows Release v0.1.0 deployed with a Site link. Click it, and run the same checklist as on test (step 5.2):

The footer shows the release, e.g. Release v0.1.0
The home page loads
Pages that read from the database show data
Login and logout work

Prod and test run the same code, so the pages work the same way. Three things differ:

Footer: test names the last merged pull request; prod names the release.
Data: each server has its own database, so data you added on test is not on prod.
Spring profile: prod uses prod; test uses test.

title: 7. Check the prod deployment
text:
7.3 Confirm which release is running
The footer is the quickest check. On a server you can log in to, such as your own practice server from step 3, you can also confirm it there:
docker ps --format '{{.Names}}  {{.Image}}  {{.Status}}'
It prints gallery  gallery:v0.1.0  Up … minutes, and gallery-db  mysql:8.4  Up … (healthy). Record the release and its date on your team’s board: this is your deployment record. Do not record the address, because it changes; the newest deploy-prod summary always has the current one.

title: 7. Check the prod deployment
text:
7.4 Roll back a bad release
If a release breaks prod, put the previous one back first and fix the problem afterwards. Rolling back changes the app only; the database and its data stay as they are.
From GitHub: open Actions → deploy-prod, click the run for the previous tag (e.g. v0.1.0) and choose Re-run all jobs. It builds and deploys that tag again, and the footer changes back to that release.
On the server, faster: your lecturer, or you on your own practice server, can start the previous image directly, since it is still there:
docker images gallery
set -a; . ~/gallery/db.env; set +a
docker rm -f gallery
docker run -d --name gallery --network gallery --restart unless-stopped \
  -p 80:8080 -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod \
  -e APP_BUILD_INFO="Release v0.1.0" \
  -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL="jdbc:mysql://gallery-db:3306/$MYSQL_DATABASE" \
  -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME="$MYSQL_USER" \
  -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD="$MYSQL_PASSWORD" \
  gallery:v0.1.0
Then fix the problem on a feature branch, check it on test, and release a new version, e.g. v0.2.1 (steps 4 to 6).






WarningNever reset the prod database



Step 5.4’s reset deletes all data. That is fine on test, but on prod it destroys real data. If prod’s data needs to change, make the change through the app, or ask your lecturer first.








WarningBefore the assessed release



Any in-memory or seed accounts in the skeleton are a week 1 convenience. Before v1.0.0 in week 11, login must use real accounts stored in the database, and test accounts must be gone from prod.

title: 7. Check the prod deployment
text:
What you have built





flowchart LR
  F["feature/*"] -->|PR + review| D["develop"] -->|auto| T["Test EC2"]
  D -->|release PR| M["main"] -->|tag v*| P["Prod EC2"]






From now on, every change follows this path: a feature branch, a reviewed pull request into develop, a check on test, then a release pull request into main and a tag to reach prod.






TipCheckpoint



The prod site, linked from the newest deploy-prod summary, serves release v0.1.0 with data from its own database and the release in its footer. Everyone can find both sites from the run summaries, and can explain how a change reaches prod.

title: Build and deploy: overview
text: In this module your team takes the Gallery skeleton from your laptops to two servers on AWS, which your lecturer runs for your team: a test server that always runs the latest develop, and a prod server that runs the latest release tag on main.

title: Build and deploy: overview
text:
The whole process





flowchart LR
  L["Laptops<br/>dev environment"] -->|push feature branch| G["GitHub<br/>team repo"]
  G -->|pull request| CI["CI workflow<br/>mvnw verify"]
  G -->|merge to develop| T["Test EC2<br/>runner + Docker"]
  G -->|tag v* on main| P["Prod EC2<br/>runner + Docker"]
















Environment
Where
Runs
Updated when
Footer shows




dev
Your laptop
Whatever branch you have checked out
You run it
local dev


test
EC2 instance with the label test
The latest commit on develop
A PR is merged into develop
PR #9: Add team cards


prod
EC2 instance with the label prod
The latest release tag, e.g. v0.1.0
A tag is pushed on main
Release v0.1.0



Each EC2 instance runs a GitHub self-hosted runner. The runner connects out to GitHub and asks for jobs; GitHub never connects in. That is why the servers only need port 80 open to the world, and why it does not matter that their public IP changes between lab sessions.

title: Build and deploy: overview
text:
The steps

Clone the team repo and run it locally
Optional: create a test server on AWS
Optional: create a prod server on AWS
Feature branches and pull requests
Check the change on the test server
Release: pull request to main and tag
Check the prod deployment

Step 1 is done by every team member, and steps 4 to 7 by the whole team.
Steps 2 and 3 are optional. Your lecturer has already built your team’s test and prod servers, so your team can deploy without them. Do them if you want to learn how a server, Docker and a GitHub runner are set up. You build your own servers for your own practice copy of the repo, so nothing you do there affects your team’s servers.

title: Build and deploy: overview
text:
Finding your team’s sites
Your lecturer runs both servers. You never need to log in to them, and you do not need to remember their addresses: every deployment posts the site’s current address on GitHub.

In your team repo, open the Actions tab.
On the left, click deploy-test for the test site, or deploy-prod for the prod site.
Click the newest run with a green tick.
The run’s summary page shows, below the job graph, Test site deployed (or Release v0.1.0 deployed) with a Site link. Click it.







TipIf the link does not answer



A server gets a new IP address whenever it restarts, for example between lab sessions, so an old summary can point at an old address. Get a fresh one:

Test: Actions → deploy-test → Run workflow, choose develop, and wait for the run to finish. It deploys develop again and posts the current address.
Prod: open the newest deploy-prod run and click Re-run all jobs. It deploys the same release again and posts the current address.

If the run stays Queued, the server is stopped: tell your lecturer.

title: Build and deploy: overview
text:
What you need

A GitHub account, with the invitation to your team repo accepted
JDK 17, Docker Desktop and Git on your laptop
For the optional steps 2 and 3 only: access to the AWS Academy course your lecturer has enrolled you in, and an SSH client (the ssh command in PowerShell, Terminal or Git Bash)







NoteFor the lecturer: before class






Create one private repo per team from the Gallery skeleton on your GitHub account, and add each student as a collaborator with Write access.
Branch protection (optional). Without it, ci.yml still runs on every pull request and shows a red cross when the build fails, but GitHub does not stop anyone merging, merging without a review, or pushing straight to develop or main. The lessons treat a green ci, one approval and no direct pushes as team rules (step 4.7), which you can check in each pull request’s history. To have GitHub enforce them, protect develop and main: require a pull request, one approval, and the build status check. On a personal account, branch protection for private repos needs GitHub Pro (free for teachers through GitHub Education).
Merge settings. In Settings → General → Pull Requests, allow both squash merging (feature pull requests, step 4) and merge commits (release pull requests, step 6).
Servers and runners. You run a test and a prod server for each team, built as in steps 2 and 3. Register each server’s runner in the team repo with the label test or prod (Settings → Actions → Runners → New self-hosted runner). Students who do the optional steps work in their own practice repo, where they are the owner and can register runners and set secrets themselves. They must never register a runner in a team repo: a second runner with the same label would take some of the team’s deployments.
Actions minutes. ci.yml runs on GitHub’s own runners and uses your account’s included minutes for private repos. The deploy workflows run on the teams’ EC2 runners and use none.
Workflows. Team repos created from the template contain ci.yml and deploy-test.yml. Add deploy-prod.yml (step 3.3) to each team repo before its first release, or the release tag deploys nothing.
Check the skeleton builds on Linux. mvnw should be committed as executable (git update-index --chmod=+x mvnw), and .mvn/wrapper/maven-wrapper.properties must be present. The workflows run chmod +x mvnw as a safety net, but cannot replace a missing wrapper file.
Footer build label. The footer needs four things in the skeleton: app.build-info: ${APP_BUILD_INFO:local dev} in application.yml, web/BuildInfoAdvice.java, templates/fragments/footer.html, and the fragment included on each page. Group00’s pull request #9 adds all four and can be copied into the skeleton. Without them the app still runs, but the footer label does not appear.
Database secrets. Each team repo needs four repository secrets, which the deploy workflows write to ~/gallery/db.env on each server: TEST_DB_PASSWORD, TEST_DB_ROOT_PASSWORD, PROD_DB_PASSWORD and PROD_DB_ROOT_PASSWORD. Only the repo owner can set them. Use letters and digits only. This generates random ones, keeps a copy in a local file (GitHub cannot show a secret again) and sets them:
repo=<owner>/<team-repo>
for s in TEST_DB_PASSWORD TEST_DB_ROOT_PASSWORD PROD_DB_PASSWORD PROD_DB_ROOT_PASSWORD; do
  v=$(openssl rand -hex 16)
  echo "$s=$v" >> "${repo#*/}-db-secrets.txt"
  gh secret set "$s" -R "$repo" --body "$v"
done
Keep the .txt file outside any Git repo. Or add each one in Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret. A server’s db.env is written only on its first deployment, so set the secrets before a server’s first deployment.

title: 6. Release: pull request to main and tag
text:
Who: the whole team decides; one person opens the release pull request and another reviews it. Goal: move what is on develop (and checked on test) onto main, and mark it with a version tag that starts the prod deployment.
Release only what you have checked on the test server (step 5). Nothing should reach prod that has not run on test first.
crumbs: 6. Release: pull request to main and tag

title: 6. Release: pull request to main and tag
text:
6.1 Choose a version number
Tags use the format vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH:



Release
Example




Your first practice release
v0.1.0


New features since the last release
v0.2.0


Only fixes since the last release
v0.2.1


The assessed release in week 11
v1.0.0



A tag can be used only once. If a release goes wrong, fix it and release the next number; never move or reuse a tag.
crumbs: 6. Release: pull request to main and tag

title: 6. Release: pull request to main and tag
text:
6.2 Open the release pull request
On GitHub: Pull requests → New pull request.

base: main ← compare: develop
Title: Release v0.1.0
Description: the list of changes since the last release. Link each merged pull request, e.g. #3, #4, #5.
Reviewer: a teammate who did not open it.

The ci check runs again, this time against main.
crumbs: 6. Release: pull request to main and tag

title: 6. Release: pull request to main and tag
text:
6.3 Review and merge
The reviewer checks that:

ci is green. GitHub would let you merge a red release, so check it yourself
The test server is running the same commit as the head of develop: compare the latest deploy-test run’s commit with the top commit in the pull request’s Commits tab
Every change in Files changed belongs in this release

Then merge with Create a merge commit, not Squash and merge. A merge commit keeps main and develop sharing the same history, so your next release pull request shows only the new changes. Do not delete develop afterwards.
crumbs: 6. Release: pull request to main and tag

title: 6. Release: pull request to main and tag
text:
6.4 Create the tag
Tag the merge commit on main by publishing a GitHub release:

On the repo’s main page, click Releases → Draft a new release.
Choose a tag: type v0.1.0 and click Create new tag: v0.1.0 on publish.
Target: main.
Release title: v0.1.0. Click Generate release notes to list the merged pull requests.
Click Publish release.







NoteOr from the command line





git switch main
git pull
git tag -a v0.1.0 -m "Release v0.1.0"
git push origin v0.1.0
Then create the release notes from the tag on GitHub, under Releases → Draft a new release → Choose a tag → v0.1.0.



Publishing the release pushes the tag, which starts deploy-prod on the prod server. Step 7 checks it.






Warning



Only tag main. If you tag a commit on develop or a feature branch, deploy-prod stops at Check the tag is on main and prod keeps running the previous release. Delete the wrong release and tag, then tag main.








TipCheckpoint



main contains the release merge commit, and the release v0.1.0 appears under Releases.
crumbs: 6. Release: pull request to main and tag

title: Welcome
text:
In the Module PJDS 07082: Multimedia Project you work in a small team to build a web application, the Gallery, and to run it the way a professional software team would. You start from a shared skeleton project, make changes on your own laptop / PC, and release them to real servers on AWS.
The focus is on the whole path from an idea on your laptop to a running site. You collaborate through GitHub, review each other’s work, and deploy automatically to a test server and then a prod server.

title: Welcome
text:
In the Module PJDS 07082: Multimedia Project you work in a small team to build a web application, the Gallery, and to run it the way a professional software team would. You start from a shared skeleton project, make changes on your own laptop / PC, and release them to real servers on AWS.
The focus is on the whole path from an idea on your laptop to a running site. You collaborate through GitHub, review each other’s work, and deploy automatically to a test server and then a prod server.

title: Welcome
text:
What you’ll learn
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

Clone your team’s repository and run the Gallery on your own laptop.
Set up and configure test and prod servers on AWS.
Use feature branches and pull requests to make changes without breaking the work of others.
Explain how a change moves from a laptop/PC to the test server and then to production.
Release a version by merging to main and tagging it, then check that it is live on the prod server.

title: Welcome
text:
How the course works
Your team works in one shared GitHub repository, and every change goes through a pull request.



Environment
Where it runs
Updated when




dev

You run it

An AWS server

text:
Where to start
Begin with the Build and deploy overview. It shows the whole process in one diagram and lists the seven steps you will follow.

title: 3. Optional: create a prod server on AWS
text:
NoteThis step is optional



Your lecturer has already built your team’s prod server. Do this step after step 2 if you want to see the release side too, in the same practice repo.
Who: you, on your own, after step 2. Goal: a second EC2 instance, with its own MySQL and a runner labelled prod, which deploys only release tags on main of your practice repo.
The prod server is built exactly like the test server. Only six things differ:
crumbs: 3. Optional: create a prod server on AWS

title: 3. Optional: create a prod server on AWS
text:
3.1 Build the server
Follow step 2 from 2.1 to 2.6, with these changes:

Use the same lab as step 2. The gallery-web security group is already there, so skip 2.2. Two t3.medium instances use your budget twice as fast: stop both when you have finished.
Name the instance gallery-prod (2.3).
Add two more secrets to gallery-practice, PROD_DB_PASSWORD and PROD_DB_ROOT_PASSWORD, different from the test ones. The first release writes them to ~/gallery/db.env on this server.

Check docker run --rm hello-world works before moving on.
crumbs: 3. Optional: create a prod server on AWS

title: 3. Optional: create a prod server on AWS
text:
3.2 Install the runner
Get a new registration token from gallery-practice, as in 2.7; tokens expire after an hour. Then on the prod server:
mkdir ~/actions-runner && cd ~/actions-runner
RUNNER_VERSION=$(curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/actions/runner/releases/latest | grep -oP '"tag_name": "v\K[^"]+')
curl -sL -o runner.tar.gz https://github.com/actions/runner/releases/download/v${RUNNER_VERSION}/actions-runner-linux-x64-${RUNNER_VERSION}.tar.gz
tar xzf runner.tar.gz
./config.sh --url https://github.com/<you>/gallery-practice --token <TOKEN> --name gallery-prod --labels prod --unattended
sudo ./svc.sh install
sudo ./svc.sh start
sudo ./svc.sh status
Check for active (running) and Listening for Jobs.






NoteHow “polling for tags” works



The runner keeps a connection open to GitHub and asks “any jobs for prod?”. GitHub only creates such a job when someone pushes a tag beginning with v. Until then, the prod server does nothing, however many times develop changes.
crumbs: 3. Optional: create a prod server on AWS

title: 3. Optional: create a prod server on AWS
text:
3.3 Add the prod workflow
If gallery-practice already has .github/workflows/deploy-prod.yml, read it and the explanations below, then go to 3.4. Otherwise add it through a pull request in your practice repo:
git clone https://github.com/<you>/gallery-practice.git
cd gallery-practice
git switch develop
git switch -c feature/add-prod-pipeline
Create .github/workflows/deploy-prod.yml:
name: deploy-prod
on:
  push:
    tags: ['v*']
concurrency: deploy-prod
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: [self-hosted, prod]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - name: Check the tag is on main
        run: |
          if ! git merge-base --is-ancestor "$GITHUB_SHA" origin/main; then
            echo "Tag ${GITHUB_REF_NAME} is not on main. Only tag commits on main."
            exit 1
          fi
      - name: Build the image
        run: |
          chmod +x mvnw
          docker build -t gallery:${GITHUB_REF_NAME} .
      - name: Write db.env from the repository secrets
        env:
          DB_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.PROD_DB_PASSWORD }}
          DB_ROOT_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.PROD_DB_ROOT_PASSWORD }}
        run: |
          if [ -f ~/gallery/db.env ]; then
            # The database keeps the passwords it was first created with, so an existing file wins.
            if [ -n "$DB_PASSWORD" ] && ! grep -qxF "MYSQL_PASSWORD=$DB_PASSWORD" ~/gallery/db.env; then
              echo "::warning::~/gallery/db.env on the server does not match the PROD_DB_PASSWORD secret. The server's file is used."
            fi
            echo "Using the existing ~/gallery/db.env"
            exit 0
          fi
          if [ -z "$DB_PASSWORD" ] || [ -z "$DB_ROOT_PASSWORD" ]; then
            echo "::error::Add the PROD_DB_PASSWORD and PROD_DB_ROOT_PASSWORD repository secrets (course step 3.1)."
            exit 1
          fi
          case "$DB_PASSWORD$DB_ROOT_PASSWORD" in
            *[!A-Za-z0-9]*) echo "::error::The database passwords must be letters and digits only."; exit 1 ;;
          esac
          mkdir -p ~/gallery
          umask 077
          printf 'MYSQL_DATABASE=idm3project2024\nMYSQL_USER=gallery\nMYSQL_PASSWORD=%s\nMYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=%s\n' \
            "$DB_PASSWORD" "$DB_ROOT_PASSWORD" > ~/gallery/db.env
          echo "Created ~/gallery/db.env"
      - name: Start the database
        run: |
          docker network create gallery 2>/dev/null || true
          if [ -z "$(docker ps -q -f name=^gallery-db$)" ]; then
            mkdir -p ~/gallery/initdb
            cp idm3project2024.sql ~/gallery/initdb/01-idm3project.sql
            docker rm -f gallery-db 2>/dev/null || true
            docker run -d --name gallery-db --network gallery --restart unless-stopped \
              --env-file ~/gallery/db.env \
              -v gallery-dbdata:/var/lib/mysql \
              -v ~/gallery/initdb:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d:ro \
              --health-cmd "mysqladmin ping -h localhost" --health-interval 5s \
              mysql:8.4
          fi
          for i in $(seq 1 60); do
            if [ "$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Health.Status}}' gallery-db)" = healthy ]; then echo "Database is up"; exit 0; fi
            sleep 2
          done
          docker logs gallery-db
          exit 1
      - name: Replace the running container
        run: |
          set -a; . ~/gallery/db.env; set +a
          docker rm -f gallery || true
          docker run -d --name gallery --network gallery --restart unless-stopped \
            -p 80:8080 -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod \
            -e APP_BUILD_INFO="Release ${GITHUB_REF_NAME}" \
            -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL="jdbc:mysql://gallery-db:3306/$MYSQL_DATABASE" \
            -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME="$MYSQL_USER" \
            -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD="$MYSQL_PASSWORD" \
            gallery:${GITHUB_REF_NAME}
      - name: Wait for the app to answer
        run: |
          for i in $(seq 1 60); do
            if curl -fs http://localhost/MainGallery/Login > /dev/null; then echo "Release ${GITHUB_REF_NAME} is up"; exit 0; fi
            sleep 2
          done
          docker logs gallery
          exit 1
      - name: Show the site address
        run: |
          # Ask AWS for this instance's public IP. It changes each time the lab restarts.
          TOKEN=$(curl -fsS --max-time 5 -X PUT http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token \
            -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 60" || true)
          IP=$(curl -fsS --max-time 5 -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $TOKEN" \
            http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/public-ipv4 || true)
          SITE=${IP:+http://$IP/MainGallery/HomePage}
          {
            echo "### Release ${GITHUB_REF_NAME} deployed"
            echo "- Site: ${SITE:-no public IP found}"
            echo "- Database: $(grep '^MYSQL_DATABASE=' ~/gallery/db.env | cut -d= -f2), user $(grep '^MYSQL_USER=' ~/gallery/db.env | cut -d= -f2)"
          } >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
          echo "Site: ${SITE:-no public IP found}"
How it differs from deploy-test.yml:

on: push: tags: ['v*'] runs it for tags such as v0.1.0, and never for branch pushes.
fetch-depth: 0 downloads the full history, so the next step can see main.
Check the tag is on main stops the deployment if someone tags a commit that has not been through a release pull request.
The image is named after the tag, e.g. gallery:v0.1.0. Older release images stay on the server, which makes rolling back possible (step 7).
-e APP_BUILD_INFO="Release ${GITHUB_REF_NAME}" puts the tag in the footer, e.g. Release v0.1.0. GitHub sets GITHUB_REF_NAME to the tag’s name, so no lookup is needed.
Write db.env from the repository secrets reads the PROD_DB_ secrets instead of the TEST_DB_ ones.
Show the site address heads the run’s summary with the release, e.g. Release v0.1.0 deployed, and links to the prod site.

Start the database is identical to the test workflow’s: the first release creates prod’s database from idm3project2024.sql, and every later release keeps its data. Prod’s data is never copied from test.
Commit, push and open a pull request into develop in gallery-practice. When ci is green, merge it yourself.
Merging it into develop does not deploy anything to prod: there is no tag yet, and the file only reaches main at your first release (step 6).
crumbs: 3. Optional: create a prod server on AWS

title: 3. Optional: create a prod server on AWS
text:
3.4 Try a release
Follow step 6 in gallery-practice: a pull request from develop into main, merged with a merge commit, then a release tagged v0.1.0 on main. The tag starts deploy-prod on your prod server. When it is green, its summary shows Release v0.1.0 deployed with a link to your practice prod site.






TipCheckpoint



Two practice servers, each with a runner listening: gallery-test (label test) and gallery-prod (label prod). Your practice prod site shows Release v0.1.0 in its footer. Stop both instances when you have finished.

title: 5. Check the change on the test server
text: Who: the author of each merged pull request, with one teammate. Goal: confirm every merged change is running on the test server before anyone builds on it.
crumbs: 5. Check the change on the test server

title: 5. Check the change on the test server
text:
5.1 Follow the deployment

On GitHub, open Actions → deploy-test. The newest run is named after your merge commit.
Click into it. Each step shows a tick as it finishes:

Find the pull request prints the footer label.
Start the database ends with Database is up.
Wait for the app to answer ends with App is up.
Show the site address prints the site’s link, which also appears on the run’s summary page.


A run usually takes two to five minutes. If it stays Queued with Waiting for a runner, the test server is not available: see the table below.
crumbs: 5. Check the change on the test server

title: 5. Check the change on the test server
text:
5.2 Check it in the browser
The run’s summary page shows, below the job graph, Test site deployed with a Site link. Click it. Always take the link from the newest run: the server’s address changes whenever it restarts (see Finding your team’s sites). Then run through this checklist:

The footer shows your pull request’s number and title, e.g. PR #7: Add Aoife to the footer
The home page loads, with the sample projects and showcases
Your change works as it did on your laptop. For your first pull request (step 4), your name is in the footer’s team list, below everyone merged before you
A test login from step 1.5 works

The footer tells you at a glance which pull request the test server is running. If it shows an earlier pull request, the deployment for yours has not finished, or failed: check Actions. Refresh with Ctrl+F5 if the page looks out of date.
crumbs: 5. Check the change on the test server

title: 5. Check the change on the test server
text:
5.3 Optional: look at the server
Only for a server you built yourself in the optional step 2; your team’s server is run by your lecturer. Connect to it (step 2.4) and run:
docker ps
docker logs --tail 30 gallery
docker ps shows two containers:

gallery, the app, on 0.0.0.0:80->8080/tcp
gallery-db, MySQL, marked (healthy) and with no published port

The app’s log ends with Spring Boot’s Started GalleryApplication.
To look inside the test database:
docker exec -it gallery-db sh -c 'mysql -u"$MYSQL_USER" -p"$MYSQL_PASSWORD" "$MYSQL_DATABASE"'
Try SHOW TABLES;, then exit.
crumbs: 5. Check the change on the test server

title: 5. Check the change on the test server
text:
5.4 Reset the test database
The test database keeps whatever data your team adds. To start again from idm3project2024.sql, for example after the team changes that file, ask your lecturer to reset your team’s test database. On a practice server of your own, run:
docker rm -f gallery-db
docker volume rm gallery-dbdata
Then open Actions → deploy-test → Run workflow and choose develop. The next deploy creates the database again from the seed file.
crumbs: 5. Check the change on the test server

title: 5. Check the change on the test server
text:
Troubleshooting
Rows marked Server need a fix on the server itself. On your team’s servers, only your lecturer can make it: send them the link to the failed run. On a practice server of your own (step 2), fix it yourself. Everything else you fix in your code, through a pull request.







What you see
Likely cause and fix




Run stays Queued, Waiting for a runner
Server. The server is stopped. Tell your lecturer. On a practice server, start the lab, then start gallery-test


The site link does not answer
The server has restarted and has a new address. Actions → deploy-test → Run workflow on develop posts a fresh link. If it still does not answer: Server, check gallery-web still allows HTTP


The summary says no public IP found
Server. The instance has no public IPv4 address (step 2.3)


permission denied … docker.sock
Server. The runner service started before ubuntu joined the docker group. On the server: cd ~/actions-runner && sudo ./svc.sh stop && sudo ./svc.sh start, then Re-run jobs


Add the TEST_DB_PASSWORD and TEST_DB_ROOT_PASSWORD repository secrets
The repo’s secrets are not set. In your team repo, tell your lecturer. In a practice repo, add them yourself (step 2.0), then Re-run jobs


The database passwords must be letters and digits only
A secret contains a symbol or space. Set it again with letters and digits only (your lecturer, in a team repo)


Warning: db.env on the server does not match the TEST_DB_PASSWORD secret
Server. The server’s file was made earlier, by hand or from older secrets. The deployment uses it and still works. To switch to the secrets: rm ~/gallery/db.env on the server, then reset the database (5.4)


App log shows HHH000342: Could not obtain connection and a NullPointerException in JdbcIsolationDelegate
The app cannot reach MySQL. Hibernate hides the real error behind this exception. Server: docker logs gallery 2>&1 \| grep -m3 "Caused by" shows it. Check gallery-db is running (docker ps), and that the app’s docker run has --network gallery and the three SPRING_DATASOURCE_ settings


Access denied for user 'gallery' in the app log
Server. db.env was changed after the database was created, and MySQL still has the old passwords. Reset the database (5.4)


Start the database times out
MySQL did not start. The step prints docker logs gallery-db: an error in idm3project2024.sql is yours to fix; a full disk (df -h) is a Server problem


./mvnw: Permission denied in the build
The workflow is missing its chmod +x mvnw line


cannot read distributionUrl property
.mvn/wrapper/maven-wrapper.properties was deleted by a pull request. Restore it with a new pull request


Wait for the app to answer fails
The app did not start. The step prints docker logs gallery: read the first ERROR or Caused by


The footer shows develop at … instead of a pull request
The commit was pushed straight to develop, not merged through a pull request; or the workflow has no pull-requests: read permission


The footer shows local dev on the server
The docker run line is missing -e APP_BUILD_INFO="$BUILD_INFO"


A page has no footer at all
That page does not include the footer fragment. Add <footer th:replace="~{fragments/footer :: footer}"></footer> before </body>


A run named after the file, e.g. .github/workflows/ci.yml, fails in 0 seconds on every push
The workflow file is empty or not valid YAML, so GitHub cannot read it. Check the file on GitHub; if it is empty, it was committed before being saved. Fix it in a new pull request


ci fails with wget: Failed to fetch …apache-maven-…-bin.zip
Maven Central refused the download. Click Re-run jobs → Re-run failed jobs. If your ci.yml has no Download Maven step, add it (step 2.8)


docker compose up --build on your laptop fails at ./mvnw with exit code 127
mvnw was checked out with Windows line endings. Your repo needs a .gitattributes file with the line /mvnw text eol=lf. Then run rm mvnw and git checkout -- mvnw



To deploy again without a new merge, open Actions → deploy-test → Run workflow and choose develop.






TipCheckpoint



The test server shows every merged change, with data from its database, the footer shows the last merged pull request and every team member’s name, and the last deploy-test run is green. develop is now ready to release.
crumbs: 5. Check the change on the test server

title: 1. Clone the team repo and run it locally
text: Who: every team member, on their own laptop. Goal: the Gallery app running on your laptop, reading the sample data from a MySQL database in Docker.
crumbs: 1. Clone the team repo and run it locally

title: 1. Clone the team repo and run it locally
text:
1.1 Check your tools
Open a terminal (PowerShell, Terminal or Git Bash) and run each check:








Tool
Check
Expect




JDK 17
java -version
17.x. IntelliJ users can skip this: IntelliJ downloads JDK 17 for you


Docker
docker --version
A version number, and Docker Desktop running


Git
git --version
A version number



You do not need Maven: the repo includes the Maven wrapper (mvnw), which downloads the right version itself.
crumbs: 1. Clone the team repo and run it locally

title: 1. Clone the team repo and run it locally
text:
1.2 Accept the invitation
Your lecturer has added you to your team’s repo on their GitHub account. Accept the invitation from the email GitHub sent you, or from https://github.com/notifications. Until you accept, the repo URL gives a 404.
crumbs: 1. Clone the team repo and run it locally

title: 1. Clone the team repo and run it locally
text:
1.3 Clone the repo
Use the URL your lecturer gives you in class. It looks like https://github.com/<lecturer>/<team-repo>.git.

IntelliJCommand line



File → New → Project from Version Control.
Paste the URL and choose a folder.
When asked, sign in with GitHub in the browser.
Click Clone, then Trust Project.
Bottom right, click the branch name (main) and choose origin/develop → Checkout.
File → Project Structure → Project: set SDK to a Java 17 JDK. If there is none, open the list → Download JDK → version 17, Eclipse Temurin.



git clone https://github.com/<lecturer>/<team-repo>.git
cd <team-repo>
git switch develop
The repo is private, so Git asks you to sign in. On Windows, a browser window opens: sign in to GitHub there. Do not type your GitHub password at a terminal prompt; GitHub rejects passwords for Git.



You work from develop, never main. main only changes at a release (step 6).
crumbs: 1. Clone the team repo and run it locally

title: 1. Clone the team repo and run it locally
text:
1.4 Start the database and phpMyAdmin
The repo’s docker-compose.yml defines three services:



Service
What it is
Address on your laptop




db
MySQL 8.4, holding the idm3project2024 database
localhost:3306


phpmyadmin
A web page for browsing and editing the database
http://localhost:8081


app
The Gallery app, built in Docker
http://localhost:8080



For day-to-day work you start only db and phpmyadmin, and run the app itself from IntelliJ or Maven (1.5).

IntelliJCommand line


Open docker-compose.yml and click the green ▶ in the gutter beside the db: service, then beside phpmyadmin:. Both appear in the Services tool window (Alt+8, or ⌘8 on a Mac). Wait until db shows healthy.
Do not start app: here: you run the app from IntelliJ in the next step, and both use port 8080.


From the repo folder:
docker compose up -d db phpmyadmin
docker compose ps
Wait until db shows healthy; run docker compose ps again if it says starting.



The first run downloads the MySQL and phpMyAdmin images, which takes a minute or two. The first time db starts, it also loads the sample data from idm3project2024.sql: users, projects and showcases.
Check the data is there. Open http://localhost:8081. If phpMyAdmin shows a login form, sign in as the app’s database user:



Setting
Value




Username / password
gallery / gallerypass


Database
idm3project2024


Root user, if you ever need it
root / rootpass



On the left, open idm3project2024. It has four tables: project, showcase, showcaseproject and user. Click user to see the sample accounts you will log in with.
From the command line, the same check is:
docker compose exec db mysql -ugallery -pgallerypass idm3project2024 -e "SHOW TABLES;"
The warning about using a password on the command line is expected.






Note



These passwords are in docker-compose.yml, in Git, so they are for your laptop only. The test and prod servers use their own passwords, stored as secrets in your team repo. phpMyAdmin is never deployed to test or prod.

title: 1. Clone the team repo and run it locally
text:
1.5 Run the app

IntelliJCommand line


Open src/main/java/idm3/project/gallery/application/GalleryApplication.java and click the green ▶ beside the class → Run ‘GalleryApplication’.
dev is the default profile. Set it explicitly anyway, so you know where the setting lives: Run → Edit Configurations → GalleryApplication → Active profiles: dev → OK.


./mvnw spring-boot:run
In PowerShell, use .\mvnw.cmd spring-boot:run. On macOS or Linux, if you get Permission denied, run chmod +x mvnw once.



Open http://localhost:8080. It redirects to the gallery home page at /MainGallery/HomePage, which lists the sample projects and showcases. Check:

The home page shows projects and showcases from the sample data
The footer reads local dev. On the servers it shows the pull request or release instead (steps 5 and 7)
You can sign in at http://localhost:8080/MainGallery/Login with a test account below




Role
Username
Password




Student

Bourke123

NoteA 404 after signing in means it worked



A successful login redirects to /dashboard, which your team has not built yet, so you see a 404 page. A wrong password keeps you on the login page with an error.


These accounts come from the sample data. Their passwords are stored as plain text, which is acceptable only on your laptop: replacing them with real, hashed passwords is part of your team’s work in weeks 2 to 4. You can also create your own student account at http://localhost:8080/MainGallery/Register.
Stop the app with Ctrl+C, or the red ■ in IntelliJ.
crumbs: 1. Clone the team repo and run it locally

title: 1. Clone the team repo and run it locally
text:
1.6 Run the build CI runs
Keep db running: the test starts the whole app, including its database connection.
./mvnw verify
(.\mvnw.cmd verify in PowerShell. In IntelliJ, open the Maven tool window → Lifecycle → double-click verify.)
It compiles the app, runs its tests and packages it. If it ends with BUILD SUCCESS, your laptop builds the app as the pipeline will. CI starts its own empty MySQL for this, so never write a test that depends on the sample data.
crumbs: 1. Clone the team repo and run it locally

title: 1. Clone the team repo and run it locally
section: 1.7 Optional: run the whole stack in Docker
text:
1.7 Optional: run the whole stack in Docker
Stop the app you started in 1.5 first, because this uses port 8080 too. Then:
docker compose up --build
This builds the app’s Docker image from the Dockerfile and runs it next to MySQL. It is close to what the test and prod servers do. Open http://localhost:8080, then stop it with Ctrl+C.
If the build fails at ./mvnw with exit code 127, mvnw was checked out with Windows line endings. Your repo needs a .gitattributes file containing /mvnw text eol=lf. Once it has one, run rm mvnw and then git checkout -- mvnw, and build again.
crumbs: 1. Clone the team repo and run it locally

title: 1. Clone the team repo and run it locally
text:
1.8 Reset your database
To throw away your local data and reload the sample data, for example after a teammate changes idm3project2024.sql:
docker compose down -v
docker compose up -d db phpmyadmin
-v deletes the database volume, so everything you added locally is gone.
crumbs: 1. Clone the team repo and run it locally

title: 1. Clone the team repo and run it locally
text:
Troubleshooting







Symptom
Fix




Repository not found when cloning
You have not accepted the invitation, or you are signed in to Git as a different GitHub account


Cannot connect to the Docker daemon
Start Docker Desktop and wait until it says it is running


Port 3306 or 8081 already in use
Another MySQL or phpMyAdmin is running, often a container from another project. Run docker ps, then docker stop <name>


Port 8080 already in use
An old run of the app is still going. Stop it in IntelliJ, or close the terminal running it


Communications link failure, or HHH000342: Could not obtain connection followed by a NullPointerException
db is not running. Start it (1.4), wait for healthy, then start the app again


Access denied for user 'gallery'
The database login in application.properties no longer matches docker-compose.yml. Both should be gallery / gallerypass


The home page is empty, or the test logins fail
The sample data did not load, usually because the database volume already existed. Reset it (1.8)


Invalid source release: 17
Your terminal or IntelliJ is using another JDK. Check java -version, or the SDK in Project Structure


maven-wrapper.properties: No such file or directory
The hidden .mvn folder is missing, usually because the project was copied rather than cloned. Clone it again


Unable to find a @SpringBootConfiguration in a test
The test is missing @SpringBootTest(classes = GalleryApplication.class)









TipCheckpoint



db is healthy, the app shows the sample projects at localhost:8080 with local dev in its footer, a test login works, and mvnw verify is green. Tell your team, and move on when everyone has reached this point.

title: 2. Optional: create a test server on AWS
text:
NoteThis step is optional



Your lecturer has already built your team’s test server, and your team’s merges deploy there without this step. To find your team’s site, see Finding your team’s sites.
Do this step if you want to learn how the server behind it is set up. You build your own server for your own practice copy of the repo, so nothing you do here affects your team.
Who: you, on your own, in your own AWS Academy lab. Goal: an EC2 instance running Docker, MySQL and a GitHub runner labelled test, which deploys the develop branch of your practice repo.
crumbs: 2. Optional: create a test server on AWS

title: 2. Optional: create a test server on AWS
section: 2.0 Make a practice copy of the repo
text:
2.0 Make a practice copy of the repo






Warning



Never register a runner in your team repo. Your lecturer’s server already serves it, and a second runner with the same label would take some of your team’s deployments.



On GitHub, click + → New repository. Name it gallery-practice, make it Private, and leave Add a README, .gitignore and license unset, so it is empty. Click Create repository.
On your laptop, in a folder outside your team clone, copy every branch and tag of the team repo into it:
git clone --bare https://github.com/<lecturer>/<team-repo>.git gallery-mirror
cd gallery-mirror
git push --mirror https://github.com/<you>/gallery-practice.git
cd ..
Then delete the gallery-mirror folder. To work on the practice repo later, clone it like any other: git clone https://github.com/<you>/gallery-practice.git.
In gallery-practice on GitHub, open Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret and add two secrets, TEST_DB_PASSWORD and TEST_DB_ROOT_PASSWORD. Choose your own values, letters and digits only.

The copy includes the team’s workflows, so a deploy-test run may appear straight away as Queued. It waits for your runner, and starts once you finish 2.7.
The practice repo is yours: you are its owner, so you can register runners and set secrets yourself. Its ci runs use your own account’s free Actions minutes.
crumbs: 2. Optional: create a test server on AWS

title: 2. Optional: create a test server on AWS
text:
2.1 Start the lab

Sign in to AWS Academy and open the course your lecturer enrolled you in (Cloud Web Application Builder).
Open the lab and click Start Lab. Wait until the dot next to AWS turns green.
Click AWS to open the AWS console. Leave the region as the lab sets it (usually N. Virginia, us-east-1).
In the lab window, open AWS Details and click Download PEM. Save labsuser.pem somewhere you can find it.







WarningBudget



Your lab account has a fixed budget. A t3.medium costs a few cents an hour while it is running. Stop the instance when your team is finished for the week, and never create more than this lesson and the next one ask for.
crumbs: 2. Optional: create a test server on AWS

title: 2. Optional: create a test server on AWS
text:
2.2 Create a security group
EC2 → Security Groups → Create security group:

Name: gallery-web
Description: Gallery app servers
VPC: the lab’s default VPC
Inbound rules:

SSH, port 22, source My IP
HTTP, port 80, source Anywhere-IPv4

Outbound rules: leave the default (All traffic to 0.0.0.0/0). The server needs it to download packages and reach GitHub.

Do not open port 3306. The database runs on the same server as the app and is never reachable from outside it.
crumbs: 2. Optional: create a test server on AWS

title: 2. Optional: create a test server on AWS
text:
2.3 Launch the instance
EC2 → Instances → Launch instances:







Setting
Value




Name
gallery-test


Image (AMI)
Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS, 64-bit (x86)


Instance type
t3.medium. A Maven build, the app and MySQL need about 4 GB of memory; smaller types run out


Key pair
vockey


Network settings → Edit
Subnet: a public subnet. Auto-assign public IP: Enable. Security group: Select existing → gallery-web


Storage
20 GiB, gp3



Click Launch instance, then open the instance and wait until Instance state is Running and Status checks pass. Copy its Public IPv4 address.






Important



If the instance has no public IPv4 address, or sits in a private subnet, it cannot reach the internet and every later step fails. Terminate it and launch again with the settings above.
crumbs: 2. Optional: create a test server on AWS

title: 2. Optional: create a test server on AWS
text:
2.4 Connect over SSH

Windows (PowerShell)macOS / Linux


The first time only, restrict the key file to your user, or SSH refuses to use it:
icacls labsuser.pem /inheritance:r /grant:r "$($env:USERNAME):R"
Then connect:
ssh -i labsuser.pem ubuntu@<public-ip>


chmod 400 labsuser.pem
ssh -i labsuser.pem ubuntu@<public-ip>



Type yes when asked about the host fingerprint. The prompt changes to ubuntu@ip-…, which means you are on the server. Every command from here to 2.7 runs on the server.
crumbs: 2. Optional: create a test server on AWS

title: 2. Optional: create a test server on AWS
section: 2.5 Check the server can reach the internet
text:
2.5 Check the server can reach the internet
curl -4 -m 5 -sI https://github.com | head -1
You should see HTTP/2 200. If the command hangs and prints nothing, the server has no internet access: check it has a public IP, that its subnet’s route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an igw- target, and that gallery-web still allows all outbound traffic.
crumbs: 2. Optional: create a test server on AWS

title: 2. Optional: create a test server on AWS
text:
2.6 Install Docker
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y docker.io
sudo usermod -aG docker ubuntu
exit
exit logs you out so the new group membership applies. Reconnect with the same ssh command, then check:
docker run --rm hello-world
It should print Hello from Docker! without needing sudo.






NoteDatabase passwords



You do not create these on the server. They are the two repository secrets you added in 2.0, TEST_DB_PASSWORD and TEST_DB_ROOT_PASSWORD. The first deployment writes them to ~/gallery/db.env on this server (step 2.8 shows how), and every later deployment reads them from there. Secrets never go into Git, and GitHub hides them if they appear in a log.
If you skipped adding them, do it now. If this server already has a ~/gallery/db.env from earlier, the deployment keeps it.
crumbs: 2. Optional: create a test server on AWS

title: 2. Optional: create a test server on AWS
text:
2.7 Install the GitHub runner
The runner is a small program that asks GitHub for jobs and runs them on this server.
Get a registration token from your practice repo. On GitHub, open gallery-practice → Settings → Actions → Runners → New self-hosted runner, choose Linux, and copy the token from the ./config.sh line in the Configure block. It expires after one hour.
Download the latest runner:
mkdir ~/actions-runner && cd ~/actions-runner
RUNNER_VERSION=$(curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/actions/runner/releases/latest | grep -oP '"tag_name": "v\K[^"]+')
curl -sL -o runner.tar.gz https://github.com/actions/runner/releases/download/v${RUNNER_VERSION}/actions-runner-linux-x64-${RUNNER_VERSION}.tar.gz
tar xzf runner.tar.gz
Register it with your practice repo, using its URL without .git, and the token:
./config.sh --url https://github.com/<you>/gallery-practice --token <TOKEN> --name gallery-test --labels test --unattended
It ends with √ Settings Saved. The runner gets the labels self-hosted, Linux, X64 and test. The test label is how the deploy workflow finds this server.
If it stops with a message about missing .NET dependencies, run sudo ./bin/installdependencies.sh and then the config.sh command again.
Install the runner as a service, so it starts again whenever the instance starts:
sudo ./svc.sh install
sudo ./svc.sh start
sudo ./svc.sh status
The status shows active (running) and, near the bottom, Listening for Jobs. Your practice repo’s runner list (Settings → Actions → Runners) shows it as Idle.






Warning



Do not run ./run.sh. It runs the runner only while your SSH session stays open; the service replaces it.
crumbs: 2. Optional: create a test server on AWS

title: 2. Optional: create a test server on AWS
text:
2.8 The workflows
Two workflow files in .github/workflows tell GitHub what to do. Your practice repo already contains both, copied from your team repo, so there is nothing to add. Read them and the explanations, so you know what your server is about to do.
.github/workflows/ci.yml runs on GitHub’s own machines for every pull request, and puts a red cross on the pull request if the build or a test fails. GitHub still lets you merge it, so the team rule is never to merge while ci is red (step 4.7):
name: ci
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [develop, main]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      db:
        image: mysql:8.4
        env:
          MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: rootpass
          MYSQL_DATABASE: idm3project2024
          MYSQL_USER: gallery
          MYSQL_PASSWORD: gallerypass
        ports: ["3306:3306"]
        options: --health-cmd="mysqladmin ping -h localhost" --health-interval=5s --health-retries=20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v5
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: '17'
          cache: maven
      - run: chmod +x mvnw
      - name: Download Maven
        env:
          MVNW_VERBOSE: "true"
        run: |
          for i in 1 2 3; do
            ./mvnw -B -v && exit 0
            echo "Download failed, retrying in 15 seconds"; sleep 15
          done
          exit 1
      - run: ./mvnw -B verify

services: db starts an empty MySQL next to the build, with the same names and passwords as your laptop’s docker-compose.yml, on localhost:3306. The app’s test starts the whole application, including its database connection, so it needs a database to connect to. These are throwaway passwords for a database that exists only for the length of the build.
The Download Maven step fetches Maven before the build and retries up to three times, because Maven Central sometimes refuses a download from GitHub’s busy shared machines. MVNW_VERBOSE makes the log show the real error if all three attempts fail.

.github/workflows/deploy-test.yml runs on the server labelled test every time something is merged into develop:
name: deploy-test
on:
  push:
    branches: [develop]
  workflow_dispatch:
concurrency: deploy-test
permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: read
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: [self-hosted, test]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Find the pull request
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: |
          INFO=$(curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $GH_TOKEN" -H "Accept: application/vnd.github+json" \
              "https://api.github.com/repos/$GITHUB_REPOSITORY/commits/$GITHUB_SHA/pulls" \
            | python3 -c 'import json,sys; prs=[p for p in json.load(sys.stdin) if p.get("merged_at")]; print("PR #%d: %s" % (prs[0]["number"], " ".join(prs[0]["title"].split())) if prs else "")' \
            || true)
          [ -n "$INFO" ] || INFO="develop at ${GITHUB_SHA::7}"
          echo "Footer will show: $INFO"
          echo "BUILD_INFO=$INFO" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
      - name: Build the image
        run: |
          chmod +x mvnw
          docker build -t gallery:test .
      - name: Write db.env from the repository secrets
        env:
          DB_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.TEST_DB_PASSWORD }}
          DB_ROOT_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.TEST_DB_ROOT_PASSWORD }}
        run: |
          if [ -f ~/gallery/db.env ]; then
            # The database keeps the passwords it was first created with, so an existing file wins.
            if [ -n "$DB_PASSWORD" ] && ! grep -qxF "MYSQL_PASSWORD=$DB_PASSWORD" ~/gallery/db.env; then
              echo "::warning::~/gallery/db.env on the server does not match the TEST_DB_PASSWORD secret. The server's file is used. Reset the test database to switch (course step 5.4)."
            fi
            echo "Using the existing ~/gallery/db.env"
            exit 0
          fi
          if [ -z "$DB_PASSWORD" ] || [ -z "$DB_ROOT_PASSWORD" ]; then
            echo "::error::Add the TEST_DB_PASSWORD and TEST_DB_ROOT_PASSWORD repository secrets (course step 2.6)."
            exit 1
          fi
          case "$DB_PASSWORD$DB_ROOT_PASSWORD" in
            *[!A-Za-z0-9]*) echo "::error::The database passwords must be letters and digits only."; exit 1 ;;
          esac
          mkdir -p ~/gallery
          umask 077
          printf 'MYSQL_DATABASE=idm3project2024\nMYSQL_USER=gallery\nMYSQL_PASSWORD=%s\nMYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=%s\n' \
            "$DB_PASSWORD" "$DB_ROOT_PASSWORD" > ~/gallery/db.env
          echo "Created ~/gallery/db.env"
      - name: Start the database
        run: |
          docker network create gallery 2>/dev/null || true
          if [ -z "$(docker ps -q -f name=^gallery-db$)" ]; then
            mkdir -p ~/gallery/initdb
            cp idm3project2024.sql ~/gallery/initdb/01-idm3project.sql
            docker rm -f gallery-db 2>/dev/null || true
            docker run -d --name gallery-db --network gallery --restart unless-stopped \
              --env-file ~/gallery/db.env \
              -v gallery-dbdata:/var/lib/mysql \
              -v ~/gallery/initdb:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d:ro \
              --health-cmd "mysqladmin ping -h localhost" --health-interval 5s \
              mysql:8.4
          fi
          for i in $(seq 1 60); do
            if [ "$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Health.Status}}' gallery-db)" = healthy ]; then echo "Database is up"; exit 0; fi
            sleep 2
          done
          docker logs gallery-db
          exit 1
      - name: Replace the running container
        run: |
          set -a; . ~/gallery/db.env; set +a
          docker rm -f gallery || true
          docker run -d --name gallery --network gallery --restart unless-stopped \
            -p 80:8080 -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=test -e APP_BUILD_INFO="$BUILD_INFO" \
            -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL="jdbc:mysql://gallery-db:3306/$MYSQL_DATABASE" \
            -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME="$MYSQL_USER" \
            -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD="$MYSQL_PASSWORD" \
            gallery:test
      - name: Wait for the app to answer
        run: |
          for i in $(seq 1 60); do
            if curl -fs http://localhost/MainGallery/Login > /dev/null; then echo "App is up"; exit 0; fi
            sleep 2
          done
          docker logs gallery
          exit 1
      - name: Show the site address
        run: |
          # Ask AWS for this instance's public IP. It changes each time the lab restarts.
          TOKEN=$(curl -fsS --max-time 5 -X PUT http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token \
            -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 60" || true)
          IP=$(curl -fsS --max-time 5 -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $TOKEN" \
            http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/public-ipv4 || true)
          SITE=${IP:+http://$IP/MainGallery/HomePage}
          {
            echo "### Test site deployed"
            echo "- Site: ${SITE:-no public IP found}"
            echo "- Footer: $BUILD_INFO"
            echo "- Database: $(grep '^MYSQL_DATABASE=' ~/gallery/db.env | cut -d= -f2), user $(grep '^MYSQL_USER=' ~/gallery/db.env | cut -d= -f2)"
          } >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
          echo "Site: ${SITE:-no public IP found}"
      - name: Remove old images
        run: docker image prune -f
What it does, step by step:

runs-on: [self-hosted, test] picks the runner with both labels: your test server.
Find the pull request asks the GitHub API which merged pull request produced this commit on develop, and saves a label such as PR #9: Add team cards. If someone pushed to develop directly, the label is develop at plus the commit’s short ID. permissions: pull-requests: read lets the workflow’s token make that call.
Build the image builds the app inside Docker from the repo’s Dockerfile: compile with the JDK, then copy the jar onto a smaller Java runtime image. chmod +x mvnw makes the Maven wrapper executable, in case it was committed from Windows without that permission.
Write db.env from the repository secrets runs only when ~/gallery/db.env does not exist yet. It writes the database name (idm3project2024), the user (gallery) and the two passwords from the repo’s secrets into that file, readable only by ubuntu. If the file is already there, it is kept: MySQL sets its passwords only when it first creates the database, so replacing them later would lock the app out. If the file does not match the secret, the run shows a warning.
Start the database creates a private Docker network called gallery. The first time, it starts a MySQL container called gallery-db on that network, using the names and passwords in ~/gallery/db.env, and loads idm3project2024.sql into it. The data lives in a Docker volume, gallery-dbdata. On every later deploy the database is already running, so the step leaves it alone and your test data survives.
Replace the running container starts the app on the same network and maps port 80 on the server to the app’s port 8080. It overrides the database settings in application.properties, which point at localhost: inside a container, localhost is the container itself. Instead the app gets gallery-db, the database container’s name on the network, plus the user and password from db.env. -e APP_BUILD_INFO passes the footer label, and --restart unless-stopped starts the app again whenever the instance restarts.
Wait for the app to answer checks the login page, which is public, for up to two minutes, and prints the app’s log if it never answers.
Show the site address asks AWS for the server’s public IP and adds a summary to the run: a link to the site, the footer label, and the database name and user. Passwords are never shown.







NoteHow this matches your laptop



Locally, docker compose up does the same job: docker-compose.yml starts a db service and sets SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL to jdbc:mysql://db:3306/idm3project2024. On the server, the workflow does it with docker run commands, and the database is called gallery-db.








NoteHow the footer works



application.properties has app.build-info=${APP_BUILD_INFO:local dev}, so the label comes from the APP_BUILD_INFO environment variable and is local dev on your laptop. BuildInfoAdvice.java adds it to every page, and templates/fragments/footer.html displays it. Pages show it by including the footer fragment:
<footer th:replace="~{fragments/footer :: footer}"></footer>
Add that line to every new page you create, just before </body>.

title: 2. Optional: create a test server on AWS
text:
2.9 Check the first deployment

If no deploy-test run is waiting, start one: in gallery-practice, open Actions → deploy-test → Run workflow and choose develop.
Click the run. The first build takes several minutes while Maven downloads its dependencies. Write db.env from the repository secrets prints Created ~/gallery/db.env, and Start the database ends with Database is up.
When it is green, the run’s summary page shows Test site deployed with a link to the site. Click it.
Check the home page lists the sample projects and showcases, and that a test login from step 1.5 works.

The footer shows develop at and the commit’s short ID, because your practice repo has no pull requests of its own yet. To see a pull request in the footer, make a small change on a branch of gallery-practice, open a pull request into develop there, and merge it.






TipCheckpoint



Your practice site loads from the link in the run’s summary, with the sample data showing. Stop the instance when you have finished, to save your lab budget.

title: 2. Optional: create a test server on AWS
text:
Between lab sessions

When the lab ends, the instance may be stopped. When you start the lab again, start the instance if it is not already running. The runner service, the database and the app start by themselves. The app may restart once while MySQL is still starting; that is expected.
The public IP changes each time the instance starts. The next deployment’s summary shows the new address; to get it without a merge, open Actions → deploy-test → Run workflow. You can also find it in the EC2 console. Update it on your board.
While the instance is stopped, deploy jobs wait in the queue as Queued. They run once the instance is back, or fail after 24 hours.
